comparison: Perfect agreement on miniML model development and performance (C3, C11-C13, C43-C46, C50). Both evaluations find the evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval provides detailed technical assessment of training dataset, architecture, and validation metrics. Peer reviewers affirm with quotes from all three reviewers describing results as 'compelling' and noting 'satisfactory level of detail.'

Perfect agreement on benchmarking results (C4, C16-C23). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the comprehensive metrics and threshold independence while acknowledging synthetic data limitations. Peer reviewers unanimously describe benchmarking as 'compelling' and note miniML 'leads to the highest detection rates' with robustness to threshold choices.

Strong agreement on generalization capability (C15, C24-C27 in OpenEval; C5, C24-C27, C53-C54 in peer review). Both find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval focuses on diversity of experimental preparations and species. Peer review includes broader claim C5 and additional biological applications (C53-C54), with Reviewer 2 providing comprehensive list of preparations where miniML succeeds.

Perfect agreement on transfer learning effectiveness (C28-C29, C51-C52, C62). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes quantitative performance comparison and practical benefits. Peer Reviewer 3 explicitly highlights this as a 'major strength' that reduces computation time and training data requirements.

Agreement on adaptation to different recording modes (C30, C61 in OpenEval; C30 in peer review). Both find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval provides detailed analysis of paired recordings validation. Peer review implicitly accepts this as part of broader generalization, with Reviewer 2 noting miniML works with 'both voltage and current clamp electrophysiology.'

Agreement on complex dataset analysis (C31-C33, C53 in OpenEval; C31-C33 in peer review). Both find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes mechanistic interpretations are inferential and would benefit from validation. Peer reviewers implicitly accept biological findings as part of demonstrating miniML's capabilities without questioning interpretations.

Agreement on Drosophila genetic perturbation results (C34-C36, C54 in OpenEval; C34-C36 in peer review). Both find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes consistency with prior literature but lack of statistical details. Peer reviewers accept genetic validation without critique, noting miniML 'presents compelling results...across experimental paradigms and species.'

Perfect agreement on optical imaging application (C37-C38, C55). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes kinetics match previous reports and power-law distribution consistency, but lacks quantitative comparison with other methods. Peer Reviewer 2 explicitly affirms miniML works with 'optically driven events using iGluSnFR3.'

Perfect agreement on voltage imaging with electrophysiological validation (C39-C42, C57). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval acknowledges 40% recall indicates room for improvement due to lower SNR. Peer reviewers accept this challenging application as demonstrating versatility, with results described as 'compelling...across experimental paradigms.'

Agreement on key advantages (C58-C60 in OpenEval; C15, C58-C60 in peer review). Both find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes automation claims are logical inferences not directly demonstrated. Peer reviewers affirm superiority and robustness, with multiple reviewers noting miniML 'should now be of considerable benefit and utility.'

Perfect agreement on training set size requirements (C14). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes this reduces annotation burden but may be specific to homogeneous training data. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this as part of satisfactory training methodology description.

Agreement on broad generalization claim (C5). Both find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes C5 is a summary supported by multiple experimental results, though 'easily' may overstate given transfer learning requirements. Peer review groups C5 with specific experimental demonstrations (C24-C27, C53-C54), with Reviewer 2 providing detailed list of successful applications.

Perfect agreement on computational efficiency (C69). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval cites specific runtime measurements from supplementary figure. Peer reviewers implicitly accept practical usability including computational efficiency, with Reviewer 2 noting software 'should now be of considerable benefit and utility.'

Perfect agreement on future directions and speculative claims (C56, C63-C64, C66, C68, C70). OpenEval classifies as UNCERTAIN, noting these are speculative but appropriately framed. Peer review classifies as SUPPORTED, accepting forward-looking statements without objection and affirming miniML 'has a great potential to become a valuable tool.'

Perfect agreement on acknowledged limitations (C65, C67). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes C65 is inherent to supervised learning and C67 is logical inference not systematically tested. Peer reviewers implicitly accept limitations as reasonable, with Reviewer 3 noting authors 'answered all claims and concerns' about training details.

Perfect agreement on background and motivation (C1-C2, C6-C10). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes these are well-accepted principles with appropriate citations. Peer reviewers accept these as standard background claims and established knowledge without question.

OpenEval evaluates methodological details (C48-C49) as SUPPORTED, describing standard recording duration and quantitative observation about iPSC cultures. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific methodological claims.
